metadata.title: How friendly are OECD countries towards children? Conceptualization and measuring issues

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study does not use ILSA microdata with sampling weights; instead, it constructs a country-level Child Friendliness Index from secondary indicators aggregated at the OECD member-country level. The authors explicitly follow Mekonen (2010) in applying equal weighting to all indicators (no indicator weighting scheme), and they do not report the use of complex survey design weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures. Because the analysis is based on secondary cross-national datasets (OECD family database, OECD How’s Life?, UNICEF, Know Violence in Childhood, ICCS 2009, and ISCIWeb Children’s Worlds 2nd wave), the concept of student-level survey weights is not applicable to the index construction. Missingness is handled by dropping countries that exceed a specified number of missing indicators within each sub-index, rather than by imputation or weight-based adjustments.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PV) handling is not applicable because the study does not estimate student-level cognitive achievement PVs for modeling; it uses country-level indicators and constructs Z-score-based composite indices. The paper also does not describe a PV-based missing-data procedure (e.g., PV pooling) because the dependent constructs are index scores derived from secondary sources rather than PV-based achievement outcomes. Missingness is addressed through country exclusion thresholds for sub-index components, but the paper does not provide a formal missing-data handling method in the sense required by PV/missing-data schema categories.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses secondary sources for 35 OECD member countries. For the nurturance and care sub-index, the final index is based on the mean of 17 indicators, but countries with more than three missing indicators in the child outcomes component are dropped from the analysis; similarly, countries with more than one missing indicator in the budgetary commitment component are dropped. For the self-determination sub-index, countries with more than three missing indicators are dropped, and the authors note that missing values in the child participation in the personal domain are a concern because no country-level indicators were available for that concept, so self-determination scores should be treated with caution. The Child Friendliness Index is computed only for countries that have scores in both sub-indices (19 countries for the final correlation analyses; 31 countries for the nurturance and care ranking table; 22 countries for the self-determination ranking table).

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2009 the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that This paper conceptualizes and operationalizes a country-level Child Friendliness Index for OECD members using secondary cross-national indicators. It combines a nurturance-and-care sub-index (17 indicators; Z-scores averaged into child outcomes and budgetary commitment) and a self-determination sub-index (6 indicators; Z-scores averaged into personal-domain participation and public-domain participation), then averages the two Z-score sub-indices into the overall Child Friendliness Index. The study uses ICCS 2009 for civic knowledge and voting intentions and uses PISA/PIRLS/TIMSS-derived school achievement indicators as part of the nurturance-and-care component, but it does not run student-level ML models or PV-based achievement prediction. Results are presented as country rankings and correlation coefficients across indices and macro indicators (e.g., GDP per capita and Gini), with Nordic countries (e.g., Finland, Sweden, Denmark) scoring highest overall. Limitations include reliance on secondary data with uneven coverage, subjective indicator selection, and missingness handled via country exclusion thresholds rather than formal imputation. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to ML-specific fields because the article is not an empirical predictive modeling study. It constructs and validates a composite index using Z-score standardization, equal indicator weighting, and correlation/ranking analyses at the country level, with no training/evaluation of machine learning algorithms and no PV-based student outcome modeling. Consequently, fields such as ml_techniques, main_findings (ML target-variable performance), and PV/missing-data handling in the PV sense are not applicable to the study’s design.
